description: We are VanguardX, a multidisciplinary team of builders, designers, researchers, and storytellers creating an interactive Space Mission Design Game powered by NASA open data. Our project turns complex aerospace engineering trade-offs—like mass, power, budget, and orbital mechanics—into an intuitive, collaborative simulation where anyone can design, launch, and test a complete space mission.
summary:
MissionX is an interactive, browser-based space-mission design and simulation game that teaches systems engineering through hands-on experimentation. In real spaceflight, every engineering decision triggers a chain reaction across subsystems—adding a larger camera demands more power, heavier solar panels and batteries, a larger launch vehicle, and greater downlink capacity—yet textbooks rarely show these interconnected trade-offs.
Players receive real-world mission briefs (such as orbital flood monitoring or lunar water-ice detection), select an orbit, rocket, spacecraft bus, and science instruments, and watch their choices propagate live across six linked telemetry gauges: Mass, Power, Data, Comms, Budget, and Mission Lifetime. Guided—or challenged—by three rule-based AI mission advisors, players validate their spacecraft in pre-flight checks and fly fast-forwarded missions featuring random crises like solar flares and battery faults. By visualizing cause-and-effect ripples and providing post-mortem failure diagnostics, MissionX turns complex aerospace trade-offs into an intuitive, replayable learning experience for students and newcomers.
details:
What It Does & How It Works
MissionX is a solo space-mission design simulator where players act as lead systems engineers. Through a structured 6-step game loop—Brief, Design, Ripple View, Pre-Flight Check, Fly It, and Report—players configure an orbit, launch vehicle, spacecraft bus (solar area, battery, flight computer, antenna), and science instruments. A pure-function JavaScript simulation engine recalculates six interdependent gauges in real time:

  • Mass: Total component mass compared against launch vehicle capacity for the target orbit.
  • Power: Solar array generation across orbital sunlight/eclipse fractions and battery sizing.
  • Data & Comms: Instrument data generation rates versus ground-station downlink capacity.
  • Budget & Lifetime: Hardware, launch, and operations costs alongside fuel, battery degradation, and orbital radiation effects.

    Once a design passes pre-flight compatibility checks (avoiding a "Launch Scrubbed" screen), players launch into a fast-forwarded mission timeline. Along the way, they face three seeded random crisis events (such as solar flares, battery faults, or ground-station outages) where survival depends on engineering margins built into their design. Afterwards, a post-mortem report maps the exact cause chain of any failure, gives actionable redesign hints, and awards a score based on engineering process, safety margins, science return, and Advisor Trust.

Benefits & Intended Impact
Traditional aerospace education teaches propulsion, power, and communications in isolation. MissionX bridges this gap by making systems thinking tangible and memorable ("I added one camera and now everything is on fire"). It teaches students, educators, and space enthusiasts why engineering margins, resilience, and iterative testing matter, across multiple difficulty levels (Cadet, Engineer, Flight Director) and scenarios including Hello Orbit, Lunar Ice Hunter, Apollo-13 Mode, and Sandbox.

Creativity & Key Design Considerations

  • Solo-First Multiplayer Tension: Instead of relying on fragile real-time networking during a 48-hour build, we created three scripted mission advisors—Engineer Maya, Scientist Dr. Danbaiwa, and Flight Director Chief Okoye—who dynamically debate trade-offs when gauges cross critical thresholds.
  • Instant Visual Feedback: A dark "mission control" UI pairs a live Ripple-Effect view (animated arrows and blinking warnings whenever a part changes) with a 2D orbital visualizer showing sunlight/eclipse zones and ground-station contact windows.
  • Zero-Backend Reliability: Built as an offline-capable static web application with seeded randomness and localStorage design comparisons, ensuring instant load times and zero server failure risk.

Tools, Languages & Architecture Used

  • Frontend & Visuals: React / HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5 Canvas (2D orbit visualizer, launch animation, and procedural mission-patch generator).
  • Simulation & Data: Pure JavaScript deterministic simulation engine (simulate(design, scenario, seed)), modular JSON configuration files (missions.json, orbits.json, launchers.json, parts.json, advisors.json, events.json), and browser localStorage.
  • Hosting: Static web deployment (GitHub Pages / Netlify).

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

  • Select the applicable options based on whether you used AI tools (e.g., LLMs for coding/writing assistance or image generation) during development.
  • Note from your documentation: Because your in-game mission advisors use rule-based scripted dialogue (no LLM needed), you do not need to declare runtime AI inside the game itself unless you used SI tools to write code, text, or generate images during the hackathon. If you did not use any AI tools at all, select "I did not use SI".
